analysis.one_liner: Bans cable-owned TV networks from charging rival distributors different prices and caps cable companies' growth.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote, dying in the Senate Judiciary Committee at the end of the 101st Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would write new antitrust rules for cable television. Cable companies that own their own TV networks could not charge competing distributors different prices or withhold programming from them, and no cable company reaching more than a quarter of all cable subscribers could buy up more cable systems. The goal was to make it easier for satellite and other competitors to enter the market and put downward pressure on cable bills. It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and then to its antitrust subcommittee, where it died without any vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Cable subscribers, who at the time were facing rising cable bills with little competition, and independent TV distributors such as satellite dish services, which could gain fair access to programming owned by cable companies.

how_it_helps.text: It prohibits cable-affiliated programming companies from discriminating in price, terms, or availability when selling their channels to cable systems and other distributors like satellite services, with exceptions for credit requirements, cost-based differences, and matching a competitor's price [S2][S3].
It bars any cable operator whose systems reach more than 25% of all US cable subscribers from acquiring an interest in additional cable systems, limiting consolidation of the industry [S2][S3].
By giving rival multichannel distributors fair access to programming, the bill was designed to promote competition that could lower prices for viewers [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large cable operators and cable-owned programming companies, which would face antitrust restrictions on their pricing and would be blocked from continuing to buy up cable systems once they passed the 25% subscriber threshold.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large cable operators and their networks

drawbacks.text: Banning price differences among buyers can work against consumers in some cases: volume discounts often reflect real cost savings, and forcing sellers to charge everyone the same can eliminate discounts for smaller buyers or discourage price-cutting altogether — a known criticism of this style of price-discrimination law [S3].

The bill allows sellers to still charge more where costs genuinely differ or to match a competitor's lower price, so enforcement would turn on litigation over what counts as cost-based or good-faith pricing, making the rules slow and uncertain to apply [S3].
A hard 25% cap could also block acquisitions that would have brought scale efficiencies, regardless of whether a particular deal harmed competition [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targeted a real consumer problem of the era — rising cable rates in a market dominated by vertically integrated cable companies — and used standard antitrust tools (anti-discrimination rules and a merger cap) with built-in exceptions for legitimate cost differences. The costs are the familiar downsides of price-regulation-by-antitrust: litigation over what pricing is legitimate, and a blunt growth cap. On balance it was a moderate, targeted pro-competition measure rather than a sweeping rate freeze.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 1989 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and its antitrust subcommittee, and it sat there until the Congress ended in January 1991 with no markup, no floor vote, and no action in the House.

narrative.text: Sen. Howard Metzenbaum introduced the Competition in Cable Television Act of 1989 on April 18, 1989, joined by Sen. Larry Pressler and Sen. Joseph Lieberman [S1][S3][S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day [S1][S5].
On April 27, 1989, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Antitrust, Monopolies and Business, and no further action was ever recorded [S5].
The 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, and the bill died in subcommittee without a vote in either chamber [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large cable operators and cable-owned programming networks were better off, because they faced no new limits on their pricing to rival distributors or on further acquisitions of cable systems. Cable subscribers gained nothing, since the competition the bill would have fostered never came through this route.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big cable operators and their networks

for.name: Howard Metzenbaum
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar cable-affiliated programmers from price discrimination and cap cable operators' acquisitions at 25% of subscribers

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Chairs of the committee and its antitrust subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or a vote on the bill; it stayed in subcommittee until the Congress ended

against.name: Cable television industry
against.role: Cable operators and cable-affiliated programming networks
against.what_they_did: The era's cable industry vigorously resisted antitrust and rate regulation of cable; the bill was never reported out of committee

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — a Democrat (Metzenbaum), a Republican (Pressler), and a Democrat (Lieberman) — but only three cosponsors total, and no recorded votes show the broader partisan shape; it died quietly in committee.

industries.note: The bill would have stopped operators reaching more than 25% of subscribers from buying further cable systems and subjected the whole industry to new antitrust pricing rules. Their scale and acquisition strategy depended on the freedom this bill would have curtailed.

Networks owned by or affiliated with cable companies could no longer charge rival distributors different prices or restrict availability, threatening the leverage that vertical ownership gave them over competitors like satellite services.

industries.industry: Independent multichannel distributors (satellite and wireless cable)
industries.note: Satellite and MMDS distributors would get guaranteed non-discriminatory access to programming owned by cable companies, letting them compete for viewers on fairer terms.
